children: OTTAWA--The Bank of Canada is increasingly confident about the domestic economy and companies' ability to navigate turbulent trade waters, adding to its conviction that it was time on Wednesday to raise interest rates.

To be sure, a sharply higher inflation outlook was a main driver in the quarter-point increase in the Bank of Canada's policy rate to 2.5%. Gov. Tiff Macklem said at a press conference following the decision that inflation now looked to be more persistent with energy prices staying higher for longer and no end to the Middle East conflict in sight. The central bank's business survey indicates a larger share of companies intend to recoup added costs through price increases in the next 12 months.

Even with that backdrop, Macklem said the economy is improving, with officials modestly upgrading their growth forecast through 2028. He said there is less slack in the economy relative to a year ago, and expects the remaining spare capacity to be absorbed during the next two years.
Less slack plus mounting cost pressures means inflation risks have intensified, Macklem said. "So we decided to increase our policy rate."

The Bank of Canada expects growth now of 1% in 2026 versus its previous 0.7% call, and 2% growth next year and in 2028 relative to sub-2% readings in an earlier forecast. The central bank's emphasis on a firmer-looking economy was an important element of the rate decision, said Frances Donald, chief economist at Royal Bank of Canada. "The rate hike isn't all about energy prices."
Donald added the central bank's upward revisions slightly exceeded Royal Bank's relatively rosy take on growth, and further rate increases wouldn't necessarily knock the economy off course.

Macklem said consumer spending has been solid, with per-capita consumption picking up steam, aided by low interest rates and stock-market gains. The central bank expects consumer spending to grow 2% next year and in 2028, arguing that higher borrowing costs will be partly offset by higher incomes, with Canada benefiting as a net exporter of crude oil.

The Bank of Canada expects the real-estate market, which last decade was a major driver of growth, to remain subdued due to slow population growth and affordability constraints. Instead, the central bank expects business investment to pick up.

Higher energy prices are drawing capital to Canada's energy patch, and Macklem said officials also expect other resource and trade-infrastructure projects categorized as national priorities by Prime Minister Mark Carney to begin rolling out. Companies are also set to ramp up spending after Carney unveiled in September an accelerated writeoff of capital equipment. "Companies aren't going to invest unless they have expected profitability," Macklem said. "Their ability to write down expenses faster will make investments more attractive."

And despite hefty U.S. tariffs on key Canadian goods and the threat of more, Macklem said Canadian exporters are performing well. Export growth broadened in the second quarter and strengthened overall, Macklem said, bolstered by robust U.S. demand, higher energy production and increasing signs that businesses are adapting to the upheaval in global trade.
The latest round of U.S. tariffs will hurt certain segments of the economy and that is set to weigh on fourth-quarter output, the central bank governor said.

Overall, Canadian firms are "finding ways to work with their U.S. clients. They're shipping more to non-U.S. destinations," Macklem said. "And when exports go up, you know businesses start to invest more to add capacity."
